old_title: Iran war live: Trump's forces may have committed war crime, says UN mission
new_title: Iran war live: Trump weighs 'big decision' after UN war crime report
old_text:
A UN fact-finding mission to Iran says it has reasonable grounds to believe US forces carried out two strikes in February that amounted to war crimes.
One of the strikes targeted a primary school in Minab, where more than 150 people were reportedly killed, including about 120 children, and another hit a sports centre in Lamerd that killed or injured 22 civilians.
"The US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen," the mission.
The report, which also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests, will be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva.
Meanwhile, Donald Trump told reporters that the US is "hopefully toward the end" of its war with Iran, adding that he has spoken with Tehran "directly".He also repeated his claim that Tehran was seeking a deal, despite Iranian officials declaring only hours earlier that peace talks will not resume until all of their conditions are met.
Iran committed crimes against humanity during protest crackdown, UN finds
The same UN report also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The probe found the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution.
Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the US and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed, and 25,000 people injured.
The government's response to the protests - including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.
UN fact-finding mission on Iran says US may have committed war crimes
The UN fact-finding mission on Iran said it had reasonable grounds to believe US forces carried out two strikes in Iran in February that amounted to war crimes - one on a primary school in Minab, where more than 150 people were reportedly killed, including about 120 children, and another on a sports centre in Lamerd that killed or injured 22 civilians.
The report will be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva.
The mission said the US had intelligence that a senior Iranian commander was at the school but failed to adequately verify the information, and found no evidence the school was being used for military purposes.
It also said the Lamerd strike was indiscriminate.
"The US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
South Korea says no decision made on military deployment to Strait of Hormuz
South Korean foreign minister Cho Hyun said on Thursday that no decision had been made on any military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz.
Cho was speaking to reporters before departing for Washington, where he is due to hold talks with US secretary of state Marco Rubio.
Earlier this month, it was reported that South Korea was considering deploying military assets to the Strait of Hormuz as it faced growing pressure from the US to do more in the Middle East.
Later, Seoul said that the military deployment was an option but clarified that nothing had been decided yet.
China calls on Iran and US to revive diplomatic process
Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi has called on Iran and the US to "rebuild the negotiation mechanism based on the consensus reached so far" and revive their stalled diplomatic process.
"We urge all parties to take effective measures to reopen the Strait of Hormuz at an early date" to safeguard the stability of international energy transport and supply chains Wang said, according to China's foreign ministry, adding that China "does not want to see regional tensions to spill over further into Yemen and the Red Sea".
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araqchi, who was on a one-day visit to Beijing, said that Tehran was "fully prepared to powerfully defend its national sovereignty and territorial integrity and safeguard its security... against aggressors" and that it "welcomes diplomatic solutions that ensure the rights of the Iranian nation".
Wang said: "The current situation once again demonstrates that the existing security architecture in the Middle East is inadequate and needs to be reformed and strengthened."
US military helping to keep Strait of Hormuz open to commercial shipping, Centcom says
Despite an ongoing blockade of Iranian maritime trade and attacks by Iran's military on commercial ships, the US military has said its forces have kept the Strait of Hormuz open to commercial shipping.
The US also claimed that they are helping facilitate the movement of hundreds of millions of barrels of oil through the strategic waterway.
On Wednesday, US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for US Central Command, said traffic through the strait "continues to flow", rejecting suggestions that Iran controls the waterway.
"Since early May, we have assisted commercial vessels moving more than 900 million barrels of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz to the global energy market," Hawkins told Al Jazeera.
The US and Iran have continued to make competing claims over who has greater control of the critical Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Iran's threat of acquiring a nuclear weapon 'taken care of', US house speaker says
US house speaker Mike Johnson has said the threat of Iran acquiring a nuclear weapon has been "taken care of".
Johnson made the remarks during a press conference in which he announced that the House would adjourn until after the midterm elections, CBS reported.
"Iran will not have a nuclear weapon," Johnson said, adding that preventing Iran from acquiring one had been "an important objective of American foreign policy for the last half-century".
"That's taken care of, and now we got to get gas prices down," he said.
Iran's national security chief says 'no trust whatsoever' in US
Iran's national security chief Mohsen Rezaei has said that Tehran has no trust in the United States, urging Washington to take practical steps to rebuild confidence.
He said Iran had "no trust whatsoever" in the United States.
This comes as Donald Trump told reporters that the US is "hopefully toward the end" of its war with Iran, adding that he has spoken with Tehran "directly".
Iran's foreign minister backs Xi's plan and hails China talks
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi called talks with Chinese officials "successful", saying Tehran values the strategic partnership it has built with Beijing.
He wrote on X: "Successful consultations in China with our partners. Iran values strategic partnership we have built over time.
"Today's decisions will decide future strategic balance in the region, with immeasurable knock-on effects.
"4 principles for peace outlined by President Xi are key."
Xi has called for peaceful coexistence, respect for national sovereignty, adherence to international law, and coordination between development and security to promote peace and stability in the Middle East.
Trump says US 'hopefully' nearing end of war
President Donald Trump told reporters that the US is "hopefully toward the end" of its war with Iran, adding that he has spoken with Iran "directly".
He also repeated his claim that Tehran was seeking a deal.
He told the crowd in North Carolina that gas and oil prices will "come down very quickly" after the war ends in Iran.
US House approves bill imposing sanctions on Iran and Russia
The US House of Representatives has passed a bill named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, voting 262-159 to impose sweeping sanctions and tariffs aimed at increasing economic pressure on Iran and Russia, Reuters reported.
The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, introduced by Graham himself, was approved by the Senate last month in an 86-11 vote.
While the legislation primarily targets Russia, it also extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996, signed by then-president Bill Clinton.
The 1996 law was due to expire in 2026 but has now been extended for another five years.
Dozens of Democratic representatives joined most Republicans in backing the bill, sending it to president Donald Trump to be signed into law.
new_text:
Donald Trump has said he faces a "big decision" on how to proceed with the Iran war, in his first remarks since a UN report said two US strikes in February may have amounted to war crimes.
The president has yet to respond directly to the UN report, but in an interview with Axios he said: "I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me."
Earlier, the UN fact-finding mission to Iran said the US struck a school in Iran "while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object".
One of the strikes targeted a primary school in Minab, where more than 150 people were reportedly killed, including about 120 children, and another hit a sports centre in Lamerd that killed or injured 22 civilians.
The report, which also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests, will be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva.
Tanker hit by projectile in Strait of Hormuz
A tanker has been hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations have said.
The strike caused a fire that has since been extinguished, with all crew reported safe and the environmental impact unconfirmed.
Traffic in the key shipping route continues to be low after Tehran all but closed it following the start of hostilities with the US.
Trump threatens 'dirty dogs' who keep leaking on Iran war
President Donald Trump has lashed out at leakers in his own administration after a series of behind-the-scenes reports on the Iran war.
As the conflict Trump claimed would be over in six weeks drags into its seventh month, insiders have repeatedly claimed the president was warned against taking action by his own advisors.

US Air Force officer recalls 'free-falling' to ground with damaged parachute after plane was shot down over Iran
Barclays predicts November interest rate hike from Bank of England, warns of more amid Middle East conflict
Barclays expects the Bank of England to raise interest rates by 25 basis points in November, citing a "dramatically changed" medium-term energy outlook, and warned that a prolonged Middle East conflict could bring further tightening.
Barclays joins JP Morgan, which also expects hikes in November and February 2027 and has similarly warned the Middle East crisis could push rates higher. JP Morgan had previously expected one hike in November followed by two cuts in 2027.
The Bank kept interest rates on hold at 3.75 per cent on Thursday, as expected, but forecast inflation could top 4 per cent early next year.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis exchanged fresh strikes across their border yesterday, widening the Middle East conflict, while the US and Iran have held no peace talks since an interim agreement collapsed weeks after being reached in June.
ICYMI: Iran sports centre was also hit in 'war crime', UN says
The UN experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd.
The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians.
It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
Iranian vice president apologises to public for economic hardship
Iran's vice president Mohammad Reza Aref has apologised to the public of the country for the economic hardship inflicted by the war with the US and Israel, saying the government is "ashamed".
"We really apologise to the people," Aref said.
"We are ashamed that today the income and expenses of our dear people, especially wage earners, do not balance."
Iran's national security chief says 'no trust whatsoever' in US
Iran's national security chief Mohsen Rezaei has said that Tehran has no trust in the United States, urging Washington to take practical steps to rebuild confidence.
He said Iran had "no trust whatsoever" in the United States.
This comes as Donald Trump told reporters that the US is "hopefully toward the end" of its war with Iran, adding that he has spoken with Tehran "directly".
US approves visas for Iranian leaders to attend UN meeting despite war stalemate
The Trump administration has granted entry visas to key Iranian figures, including the country's president and foreign minister, enabling them to attend next week's UN General Assembly high-level sessions in New York despite an ongoing conflict between the two nations.
On Thursday, the State Department confirmed that visas had been issued for Iran's core delegation and essential support staff. According to US officials speaking on condition of anonymity due to visa privacy laws, the main delegation features President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The decision comes amidst an extraordinary backdrop of a military stalemate lasting over six months, with no immediate indications of progress toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz or resuming diplomatic talks regarding Iran's nuclear program.
